coach_says: Your knight on d4 was only defended by the queen, and Bd3 put the bishop right in the queen's way on the d-file, so Black simply takes Nxd4 and you can't recapture. Before you develop a piece, check whether it cuts off the defence of something else. Here Nxc6 (or f3 to hold e4 first) keeps everything protected.
concept: blocked the queen's defence of d4

coach_says: c2 looks scary, but White just answers Rc1, the pawn is blockaded and stuck, and the knight and king come over to win it. A passed pawn that has run ahead of its support and is blockaded becomes a target. Rc5 was stronger: it kicks the knight off d5 with tempo, keeps the pawn on c3 where your rook still guards it, and then Ra5 goes after a2.
also: gain time by attacking the knight

coach_says: White's knight on f3 was already attacking your e5 pawn, and Bc5 develops a piece but leaves e5 unprotected, so Nxe5 just wins a pawn. Before developing, ask what your opponent's last move attacks. Nc6 or d6 guards e5 and develops at the same time.

White's king has no castled shelter and the f and g pawns are gone, so it's time to hit it with checks. Qh4+ forces Kd2, because Ke2 loses the queen to Bxf3+, and the king is stuck in the middle while you bring more pieces. b5 just protects a pawn that wasn't in danger and gives White time to tidy up with h4.
concept: attack the exposed king with checks
also: slow move when the enemy king is open

coach_says: Your rook on d3 was attacked by the king, but White's bishop on c6 was also undefended. Instead of just retreating, take with check first: Rxd2+ Rxd2 Rxc6, and you've swapped your rook for both bishops. When your piece is going to be lost or must retreat, see if it can grab something on the way out.

Your knight had to move because of c4, and Nc5 aims at b7 but Black just plays b6 and the knight has to go to a6 on the edge, where it does nothing while the c-pawn lives on. Ne5 was much better: from the centre it attacks the c4 pawn, works with your rook on e7 against f7, and can drop back to d3 to stop the pawn. Before you put a knight somewhere, check whether a pawn can kick it to a worse square.

The bishop had to move, but on d3 it blocks your d-pawn and your dark-squared bishop, and Black develops easily with Bd6, Nge7 and castling. With the e-file open and Black's king still in the centre, Re1+ first makes Black block with the bishop, then Bb5 pins the c6 knight. Use the open file while the king is still uncastled, and avoid parking a bishop in front of your d-pawn.
also: check on the open e-file first

coach_says: After Bxe5 fxe5 the pawn lands on e5 and attacks your f6 knight, and that knight is what holds d5 against Bb3 and the rook on d1. So the trade gives White a pawn that hits your defender, and your knights get tangled. Rad8 was calmer: it puts another guard on d5 and you can take on e5 later when it suits you.

Your knight on g5 was attacked by h6, and Bh7+ doesn't solve that: after Kh8 both the bishop and the knight are attacked, so the bishop must go back to d3 and Black gets a free Ne5 hitting it. You end up trading off your good bishop and getting doubled d-pawns. A check that leads nowhere just loses time; here simply retreat with Nf3.

Good move. Your bishop on b1 was lost to the rook on f1 anyway, so d5 hits the bishop on c4 and gets a piece back. When a piece of yours is trapped, look for a counterattack like this before giving up.
Fine move: developing the knight is about as good as anything here. You're already a piece down, so the job is to bring pieces out and look for chances against White's king in the centre.
Be2 is a solid move that breaks the pin idea and keeps your structure. Bc4 was a touch more active, but there's nothing to learn from the difference here: go and win the d4 pawn.
Kd3 is fine and you're still winning comfortably. Ba3 heading round to win f4 was slightly cleaner, but the plan is the same: pick up the loose kingside pawns and push the d-pawn with king support.

The knight on e5 was attacking your bishop on c4, and f4 attacks the knight back, but it simply takes Nxc4 first. You don't lose material, but you give up your bishop pair and loosen your king's pawns. When a piece is attacked, a counterattack only works if the attacker can't just take; here Bb3 keeps both bishops.

You saw the rook on d8 hitting your d2 bishop, but your bishop on c6 was also undefended. After Rd1, Rb6 attacks it and White ends up giving back a piece. Nd4 does both jobs at once: it blocks the d-file in front of d2 and protects c6. When you have two loose pieces, look for one move that guards both.
also: one move that solves two problems

coach_says: Your e6 pawn is pinned to your queen on the e-file, so the f5 pawn was really only held by the rook. Pushing f4 hits the queen, but after Qe4 White threatens both Qxa8 and Qxh7+, and once you deal with that the f4 pawn just falls. Nc6 first guards your queen, which frees e6, and keeps your extra pawn.

Your e5 pawn was attacked twice, by d4 and the knight, and d5 doesn't defend it, so Nxe5 wins a pawn for free. In this opening Black has to deal with e5 straight away: push it with e4 or trade with exd4.

Black's bishop on g4 had just taken your knight and was attacking your queen. Bxd6 grabs a bishop but Bxd1 takes your queen. When your queen is attacked, deal with that first: Qxg4 recaptures the piece and you're fine.
concept: missed that the queen was attacked

coach_says: White's queen on e4 and bishop on c2 line up at h7, and Qe4 threatened both Qxa8 and Qxh7+. Nb6 covers the rook but walks into Qxh7+ and a mating attack. Nf6 was the move: it blocks the h7 attack and the long diagonal at once, and hits the queen.
concept: missed the queen and bishop on h7

coach_says: Qf3 puts the queen on a square where Ne5 attacks it with tempo, and the knight lands on a great central square. f4 was the plan: it controls e5 so the knight can't come there, and it attacks the g5 pawn that Black weakened with g5. Before moving the queen, check whether a minor piece can chase it.
